prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, trapping many atoms at the magic wavelength to reach unprecedented precision in the measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the one candidate on the list where all eight members already agree on the laureate pair and where the physics is as secure as it gets. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the light shift that would otherwise destroy the accuracy of a trapped-atom clock, and Ye's group turned it into a many-body, quantum-limited instrument with fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. Independent laboratories in Japan, the US, France, Germany and elsewhere have reproduced and compared these clocks, and the frequency-ratio campaigns give exactly the kind of agreement between theory and experiment that I trust. The results are used to test relativity, search for varying constants and dark matter, and measure gravitational redshift across millimetres, and they underpin the coming redefinition of the second. It is a discovery about how well nature can be controlled, built on clean quantum mechanics, and a two-person prize is naturally tidy.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the field has been recognised twice in adjacent forms, the optical frequency comb in 2005 and the control of single trapped ions in 2012, so some colleagues may see lattice clocks as a refinement of established metrology rather than a new discovery. There is also a credit-boundary risk, since Lemonde, Gill, Hollberg, Ludlow and the ion-clock groups made decisive contributions that two names cannot cover, and the SI redefinition is not yet complete, which could argue for waiting. I also have to admit that a precision-measurement prize speaks less directly to the quantum-classical boundary than some of the alternatives.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks optical lattice clocks only seventh and suggests that it may be better to wait for the redefinition of the SI second.
responses.response: I do not think the redefinition should set the timing. The Nobel standard is that the discovery is established and reproduced, and it is: several laboratories have reached the 1e-18 level and international comparisons are routine. The prize recognises the physics of the magic-wavelength lattice and the quantum-limited many-atom interrogation, not a metrological convention decided by the CGPM. I agree with Mehlig that the 2005 comb prize needs careful framing in the citation, and that is why I would word it around the lattice concept and its realisation rather than timekeeping in general.

responses.point: Olsson puts magic-angle graphene first and calls it a new platform that nobody could see or tune before, while placing optical lattice clocks third as a compact and defensible pair.
responses.response: I take the platform argument seriously, and I accept that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiments is a clean theory-plus-experiment story. My disagreement is about maturity. After about eight years the pairing mechanism is still unsettled and the credit boundary excludes Cao and the other experimental co-leads, whereas the lattice-clock performance claims have been checked by independent groups for two decades. Being a field that others have reproduced and built on matters more to me than being the most fashionable one. I would be content with B015 as my alternative if the committee finds clocks too incremental.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B053 first as a conceptual shift and treats optical lattice clocks (rank 6) as a clean but possibly incremental continuation of 2005 and 2012 metrology, with a question whether it is discovery or engineering.
responses.response: I respect the conceptual weight of topological insulators, but I think the engineering label misdescribes lattice clocks. The magic-wavelength trick is a physics idea, a choice of wavelength where the differential light shift cancels, and the many-body effects (collisional shifts, spin-orbit coupling, correlated lattice gases) were learned and then exploited. The 2005 prize gave us the comb, which is the ruler, and the 2012 prize gave us ion control, a different architecture. Lattice clocks are a third thing. I do agree that the topological-insulator credit set is the worse problem, since leaving out Mele or Zhang is awkward, and that point counts against B053 for me.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first and atom interferometry second, describing both as measurement-limited progress that opens new sensing capabilities.
responses.response: I share the first two choices, but I think we should not merge the arguments. Lattice clocks have a clean two-person attribution and the performance is decisive, while atom interferometry has contested credit among Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich, Chu and Mlynek and the 1997 laser-cooling prize overlaps it. I would also qualify Kroll's emphasis on geodesy and applications, because for me the persuasive part is the fundamental physics of coherent control of many atoms, not the field-deployable devices. I therefore keep B035 as an alternative rather than as a joint prize.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as an instrument-driven opening of a new observational window and optical lattice clocks second, noting that earlier prizes limit the overlap.
responses.response: I agree with Pearce that control of systematics and independent reproduction are what make clocks convincing. On IceCube, I would defer to colleagues on particle and astroparticle physics, but I notice that Pearce himself flags that source identification is only at the 3 to 4 sigma level for individual objects and that the credit set leaves the AMANDA pioneers open, which weakens the maturity case compared with clocks. I disagree that the overlap with earlier prizes is limited, however, and I think we should be explicit about this in the citation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that lattice clocks are distinct enough from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.

Whether the credited pair adequately represents groups outside Katori and Ye (for example Lemonde, Gill, Hollberg, Ludlow, and ytterbium and strontium efforts), and how to weight the magic-wavelength proposal against later accuracy records.
I cannot independently verify the latest stated uncertainty figures or the timetable for the redefinition of the second.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for Katori or Ye. I work in theoretical atomic physics and have a long-standing collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, but that does not connect to lattice clocks. Atom interferometry (my alternative B035) and ultracold lattices (B005) are in the neighbouring AMO community, and I have no known tie to Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich, Müller or the optical-lattice group names.
